'''Mayo''', known natively as {{lang|mfy|Yorem Noki}}, is an [[Uto-Aztecan languages|Uto-Aztecan]] language. It is spoken by about 40,000 of the [[Mayo people|Mayo]] (Yoreme) people, who live in the southern portion of the [[List of states of Mexico|Mexican state]] of [[Sonora]] and in the north of the neighboring state of [[Sinaloa]]. Under the [[General Law on the Linguistic Rights of Indigenous Peoples]], it is recognized as a "national language" along with 63 other indigenous languages and [[Spanish language|Spanish]] which all have the same validity in Mexico. The language is considered 'critically endangered' by UNESCO.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unesco.org/languages-atlas/|title=UNESCO Atlas of the World's Languages in danger|website=www.unesco.org}}</ref>

The Mayo language is partially intelligible with the [[Yaqui language]], and the division between the two languages is more political, from the historic division between the Yaqui and the Mayo peoples, than linguistic.

Programming in both Mayo and Yaqui is carried by the [[National Institute of Indigenous Peoples|INPI]]'s radio station [[XEETCH-AM]], broadcasting from [[Etchojoa|Etchojoa, Sonora]].

== Alphabet ==
The mayo alphabet contains the following letters

a, b, c, ch, e, gu, hu, i, j, l, m, n, o, p, qu, r, s, t, u, y, '<ref>{{Cite book |last=Collard |first=Elisabeth Scott |url=http://archive.org/details/rosettaproject_mfy_ortho-1 |title=Mayo Orthography |date=1974 |publisher=Instituto Linguistico de Verano |others=The Long Now Foundation}}</ref>

==Morphology==
Mayo is an [[Agglutination|agglutinative]] language, where words use suffix complexes for a variety of purposes with several [[morpheme]]s strung together.
